title: 2 Kings 12:1–16
context: Jehoash, also called Joash in the WEB, reigns forty years in Jerusalem and does what is right in the LORD’s eyes while Jehoiada the priest instructs him, though the high places are not removed. He orders the priests to use the temple income for repairs. By his twenty-third year the repairs have not been made, so he changes the arrangement. Jehoiada sets up a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar, and the collected money is counted and paid directly to the workmen, who deal faithfully. The money from guilt and sin offerings remains the priests’. Numbering note: WEB 12:1–21 corresponds to Hebrew 12:2–22, because WEB 11:21 is Hebrew 12:1; the WEB numbering is kept here. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:1–14 tells the repair story with some differences, such as placing the chest at the gate. Both traditions read the account as narrative: real reform, care for God’s house and honest administration, alongside an incomplete removal of false worship.

verses.text: Jehoash began to reign in the seventh year of Jehu, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah of Beersheba.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash begins to reign in Jehu’s seventh year and reigns forty years in Jerusalem; his mother is Zibiah of Beersheba. The regnal formula begins his reign.

Arminian readers note that the long reign gave Jehoash many opportunities to lead the people faithfully, and that the narrative will show both the good he did and the ways he fell short.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the synchronism with Jehu links the histories of Judah and Israel, and that the long reign of David’s heir, once nearly destroyed, testifies to God’s preserving faithfulness. This is Hebrew 12:2, since WEB numbering runs one verse behind here.

Both traditions read the verse as the formal introduction to his reign.

verses.text: Jehoash did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes all his days in which Jehoiada the priest instructed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash does what is right in the LORD’s eyes all his days in which Jehoiada the priest instructs him. His faithfulness is linked to his teacher.

Arminian readers note that the phrasing may hint that his faithfulness depended on Jehoiada’s influence, and the parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:2 says all the days of Jehoiada, which suggests a change after the priest’s death.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Hebrew can be read either as limiting his good conduct to the years of Jehoiada’s instruction or as describing his whole life as shaped by that instruction; interpreters differ, and Chronicles supports the former.

Both traditions honor the role of godly instruction and see the verse as a warning about faith that rests on another’s strength.

verses.text: However, the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.
verses.arminianNotes:
However, the high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense there. The reform is incomplete.

Arminian readers note that the persistence of the high places shows that the king’s reform did not go as far as it should, and that partial obedience leaves room for later decline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this recurring notice in Kings (compare 1 Kings 15:14; 22:43) measures each king against the standard of worship at the place God chose (Deuteronomy 12:5), and that even good kings left work undone until Hezekiah and Josiah.

Both traditions read the verse as a sober qualification of an otherwise good reign.

verses.text: Jehoash said to the priests, “All the money of the holy things that is brought into the LORD’s house, in current money, the money of the people for whom each man is evaluated, and all the money that it comes into any man’s heart to bring into the LORD’s house,
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash tells the priests that all the money for holy things brought into the LORD’s house, the money from assessments, and freewill offerings is to be used for repairs. The king takes initiative.

Arminian readers note that the king’s concern for the temple reflects genuine devotion, and that his plan draws on the regular income from census money (compare Exodus 30:12–16), valuations of vows (Leviticus 27:1–8) and voluntary gifts.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the temple, damaged under Athaliah’s influence (compare 2 Chronicles 24:7), needed restoration, and that the king’s command shows concern for the place where God had set his name.

Both traditions read the initiative as a good work of reform.

verses.text: let the priests take it to them, each man from his donor; and they shall repair the damage to the house, wherever any damage is found.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests are to take the money, each from his donor, and repair the damage to the house wherever it is found. The plan relies on the priests.

Arminian readers note that the arrangement placed responsibility on the priests to act faithfully, and that the outcome in the next verses shows how good plans can fail when those responsible do not carry them out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the priests were entrusted with both receiving and using the funds, and that the narrative does not state why the work was delayed; readers should not supply motives the text does not give.

Both traditions read the verse as a practical arrangement that will need correction.

verses.text: But it was so, that in the twenty-third year of King Jehoash the priests had not repaired the damage to the house.
verses.arminianNotes:
By the twenty-third year of King Jehoash, the priests have not repaired the damage to the house. Years pass without progress.

Arminian readers note that the delay shows how even religious leaders can neglect their responsibilities, and that faithfulness in practical matters is part of serving God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the text simply records the failure without explaining whether it came from neglect, competing needs or poor administration, and that the king’s response in the next verse addresses the problem directly. Jehoash would by then have been about thirty.

Both traditions read the delay as narrative that sets up a needed reform.

verses.text: Then King Jehoash called for Jehoiada the priest, and for the other priests, and said to them, “Why aren’t you repairing the damage to the house? Now therefore take no more money from your treasurers, but deliver it for repair of the damage to the house.”
verses.arminianNotes:
King Jehoash summons Jehoiada and the other priests, asks why they are not repairing the house, and tells them to take no more money from their treasurers but to hand it over for the repairs. The king corrects the process.

Arminian readers note that the king holds even the priests accountable, showing that leadership includes the responsibility to correct failures.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king’s question to Jehoiada, his own mentor, shows that the work of God’s house required accountability from everyone, and that God’s institutions are served by sound administration as well as good intentions.

Both traditions see the correction as a fitting act of responsible leadership.

verses.text: The priests consented that they should take no more money from the people, and not repair the damage to the house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests agree to take no more money from the people and not to be responsible for the repairs themselves. The roles are separated.

Arminian readers note that the priests accept the new arrangement, which removes them from handling the repair funds, and that humility in accepting correction is a mark of faithful service.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the separation of the priests from the repair funds creates a clearer system, and that the narrative presents this as a practical solution rather than a judgment on the priesthood as a whole.

Both traditions read the agreement as a constructive step in the reform.

verses.text: But Jehoiada the priest took a chest and bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one comes into the LORD’s house; and the priests who kept the threshold put all the money that was brought into the LORD’s house into it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada takes a chest, bores a hole in its lid, and sets it beside the altar on the right as one enters the LORD’s house, and the doorkeeping priests put in all the money brought. The chest makes giving transparent.

Arminian readers note that the chest provides a visible and trustworthy way for the people to give, encouraging generosity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:8 places the chest outside at the gate and mentions a proclamation, and that the two accounts emphasize different details of the same reform.

Both traditions see the chest as a wise means of honest stewardship, and neither builds a doctrine on the method of collection.

verses.text: When they saw that there was much money in the chest, the king’s scribe and the high priest came up, and they put it in bags and counted the money that was found in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
When there is much money in the chest, the king’s scribe and the high priest come, bag it and count it. The counting is shared.

Arminian readers note that the involvement of both a royal official and the high priest provides accountability, a practical safeguard against misuse of funds given to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the people’s response fills the chest, and that God’s house is restored through the generosity of his people and the careful oversight of both civil and religious leaders.

Both traditions read the verse as a picture of faithful stewardship in which generosity and accountability work together.

verses.text: They gave the money that was weighed out into the hands of those who did the work, who had the oversight of the LORD’s house; and they paid it out to the carpenters and the builders who worked on the LORD’s house,
verses.arminianNotes:
They give the weighed money to those who oversee the work on the LORD’s house, who pay the carpenters and builders working on it. The money goes directly to the work.

Arminian readers note that the funds are put to their intended use without delay, showing that faithful administration turns generous giving into real results.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the skilled labor of carpenters and builders is honored as service to the LORD’s house, reflecting a biblical view that ordinary work can be done for God’s glory (compare Exodus 31:1–6).

Both traditions see the verse as an example of faithful work in God’s service.

verses.text: and to the masons and the stone cutters, and for buying timber and cut stone to repair the damage to the LORD’s house, and for all that was laid out for the house to repair it.
verses.arminianNotes:
The money also pays masons and stonecutters and buys timber and cut stone to repair the LORD’s house, and covers all the costs of the repair. The work is thorough.

Arminian readers note that the detailed list of workers and materials shows the care taken to restore the house properly, and that faithfulness in practical details honors God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the restoration of the temple through these means reflects God’s concern for the place where his name dwelt, and that the narrator records the work with evident approval.

Both traditions read the verse as a positive account of the repair, without theological dispute.

verses.text: But there were not made for the LORD’s house cups of silver, snuffers, basins, trumpets, any vessels of gold or vessels of silver, of the money that was brought into the LORD’s house;
verses.arminianNotes:
But no silver cups, snuffers, basins, trumpets, or gold and silver vessels are made for the LORD’s house from the money brought in. The priorities are clear.

Arminian readers note that the decision to focus on structural repairs rather than new vessels shows wise prioritizing of urgent needs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the parallel in 2 Chronicles 24:14 says vessels were made from what remained after the repairs were finished, so the two accounts may describe different stages; interpreters harmonize them in this way, though the details are not certain.

Both traditions read the verse as narrative about stewardship.

verses.text: for they gave that to those who did the work, and repaired the LORD’s house with it.
verses.arminianNotes:
For they give the money to the workmen and repair the LORD’s house with it. The purpose is fulfilled.

Arminian readers note that the repetition emphasizes that the money was used for its intended purpose, a mark of integrity that God’s people should practice in all their giving and spending.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the restoration of the house through the faithful use of the people’s gifts is a sign of God’s blessing on the reform, and that his house is restored through ordinary means faithfully used.

Both traditions see the completed repair as a good work and a fitting response to God’s preservation of David’s line.

verses.text: Moreover they didn’t demand an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money to give to those who did the work; for they dealt faithfully.
verses.arminianNotes:
They do not require an accounting from the men who receive the money to pay the workers, because they deal faithfully. The overseers are trusted.

Arminian readers note that the trustworthiness of the overseers is commended, and that integrity in handling resources builds trust and makes elaborate controls unnecessary.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator highlights faithful dealing, a quality Scripture prizes in stewards (compare 1 Corinthians 4:2), and that such faithfulness is itself a fruit of God’s work among his people.

Both traditions honor the integrity of the overseers.

verses.text: The money for the trespass offerings and the money for the sin offerings was not brought into the LORD’s house. It was the priests’.
verses.arminianNotes:
The money from guilt offerings and sin offerings is not brought into the LORD’s house; it belongs to the priests. The priests’ portion is preserved.

Arminian readers note that the reform respects the provision the law made for the priests (compare Numbers 5:8–10; 18:8–9), so that care for the house does not deprive those who serve in it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the distinction between repair funds and the priests’ portion shows that the reform worked within the framework of the law, honoring both the house of God and those who ministered there.

Both traditions read the verse as a fair arrangement, and neither builds a doctrinal dispute on the method of funding.
